Why the smartest leaders in 2026 are deliberately going blind to data — and winning
I fired my Chief of Staff’s dashboard habit in March.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Not the person. The habit. Eighteen months of quarterly obsession over churn curves, NPS deltas, and Slack sentiment scores, and I finally told her: stop sending me the deck before every decision. She looked at me like I’d asked her to fly the plane blindfolded.
Here’s the truth nobody at the leadership conferences wants to say out loud: the “data-informed decision-making” gospel that’s dominated executive training for a decade is quietly wrecking the judgment of an entire generation of leaders. And 2026 is the year the bill comes due.
The Consensus Everyone’s Selling
Walk into any leadership summit right now and you’ll hear the same three-part sermon. First, build an AI policy so your teams use tools responsibly. Second, cultivate psychological safety because Wiley’s research shows psychologically safe teams are 31% more likely to be high performers. Third, blend human judgment with machine-generated insight — the “Human and AI partnership” model DDI is pushing as the defining leadership trend of the year.
It’s not wrong advice. It’s just incomplete, and incompleteness at the executive level is where companies quietly bleed out.
Every consultancy from LHH to Harvard Business is converging on the same message: leaders need better inputs. More data. More AI augmentation. More continuous feedback loops. Joshua Bersin calls this the shift from “do it well” to “do it now,” an embrace of iteration over perfection because AI-era decisions can’t wait for certainty. Fine in theory. In practice, I’ve watched it produce something else entirely: executives who’ve outsourced their spine to a spreadsheet.
The Gap Nobody’s Naming
Here’s what twenty years in operating rooms — boardrooms, I mean, though some days it feels the same — has taught me. The leaders drowning right now aren’t drowning in a lack of data. They’re drowning in an excess of it, and they’ve mistaken more inputs for better decisions.
I watched a VP of Ops at a mid-market logistics firm spend forty minutes in a leadership sync last quarter trying to decide whether to greenlight a warehouse automation pilot. Forty minutes. He had six dashboards open. Sentiment analysis on the floor staff. AI-generated risk scores. A consultant’s slide deck modeling three scenarios. He had everything except an opinion.
That’s decision fatigue’s real mechanism in 2026, and it’s not the classic “too many choices” fatigue from behavioral economics textbooks. It’s inversion fatigue: the exhaustion of holding a conviction long enough to test it against ten conflicting data streams, all curated by tools designed to sound authoritative regardless of whether they’re actually right. The Forbes leadership pivot pieces call this the “psychological safety era,” but nobody’s asking the harder question — psychological safety for whom, when the leader themselves can’t commit to a call?
Trust research backs this up in a way the HR consultancies gloss over. Bersin notes American institutional trust has cratered from 80% in the 1960s to 17% today. Everyone reads that stat and concludes: leaders need to rebuild trust with employees. True, but secondary. The primary fracture is leaders’ trust in their own pattern recognition. When you’ve spent five years being told the model knows better, you stop trusting the twenty years of scar tissue that actually taught you something.
The Contrarian Move
So here’s the gap. While the industry tells you to build better AI-human partnerships, the executives actually winning right now are doing something almost heretical: they’re scheduling deliberate data blackouts before high-stakes calls.
Not permanently. Not as a personality quirk. Strategically.
A CFO I advise — runs finance for a 400-person manufacturing group — instituted what she calls “naked decisions” last year. Before any capital allocation above $500K, she requires the proposing team to walk in without slides. No dashboards. Just the thesis, spoken, defended in real time. She told me flat out: “The moment someone hides behind a chart, I know they haven’t actually thought it through.” Her capital deployment mistakes dropped by nearly a third in twelve months. Not because she got smarter data. Because she forced conviction to surface before evidence could paper over its absence.
This isn’t anti-AI. It’s anti-abdication. The DDI framework of “human and AI partnership” assumes both partners show up with something to contribute. Most executives right now show up to that partnership having already surrendered their half of the negotiation.
Where This Actually Bites
The mid-management layer is where this gap compounds fastest, and it’s exactly the cohort every 2026 leadership report says needs empowering. You cannot empower a manager to make judgment calls if you’ve spent three years training them that judgment calls are what you do before you check the dashboard, not instead of it. Empathy and feedback culture, both rightly emphasized across this year’s leadership research, mean nothing if the underlying skill — deciding under incomplete information — has atrophied.
Rebuilding it isn’t complicated, but it’s uncomfortable. It means normalizing being wrong in public, faster, before the data arrives to protect you. It means promoting the person who called it right with 60% of the information over the one who was right with 95%, three weeks too late to matter. Most cultures reward the opposite.
The Hard Truth
Data was never supposed to replace judgment. It was supposed to test it. Somewhere in the last five years, executives flipped that relationship, and now an entire layer of leadership can’t recognize its own instincts anymore because it never lets them run unsupervised.
The leaders who’ll actually thrive through this AI transition aren’t the ones with the best dashboards. They’re the ones who can still tell you, without opening a single tab, exactly what they think — and why they’d bet their job on it.
